You apply the specific \"cure\" (the mathematical substitution/recipe) for that type.\n\nHere is your step-by-step, 3-day syllabus tailored directly to your PDF.\n\n---\n\n### **Day 1: The Bread and Butter (1st Order DEs)** *~6.5 Hours*\n*Goal: Master the three most common 1st-order equations.*\n\n*   **Hour 1-2: Separable DEs (DE z ločljivima spremenljivkama - Ch 2.1)**\n    *   *Form:* $y\u0027 \u003d f(x)g(y)$\n    *   *Recipe:* Put all $y$\u0027s and $dy$ on one side, all $x$\u0027s and $dx$ on the other. Integrate both sides. Don\u0027t forget $+ C$.\n*   **Hour 2-3.5: Homogeneous DEs (Homogena DE - Ch 2.2)**\n    *   *Form:* $y\u0027 \u003d f(\\frac{y}{x})$\n    *   *Recipe:* Introduce a new variable $u \u003d \\frac{y}{x}$ (so $y \u003d ux$ and $y\u0027 \u003d u\u0027x + u$). This magically transforms it into a Separable DE!\n*   **Hour 3.5-6.5: Linear DEs of 1st Order (Linearna DE prvega reda - Ch 2.3) 🔥 *CRITICAL***\n    *   *Form:* $y\u0027 + f(x)y \u003d g(x)$\n    *   *Recipe:* First solve it as if $g(x) \u003d 0$ to get the homogeneous solution $y_H \u003d C \\cdot e^{-F(x)}$. Then use a genius trick called **Variation of Constants (Variacija konstant)**, where you pretend $C$ is actually a function $C(x)$, and plug it back in to find the particular solution $y_P$.\n\n### **Day 2: Sneaky 1st Order \u0026 Intro to Higher Order** *~7 Hours*\n*Goal: Learn the substitution tricks for advanced 1st order, and learn the ultimate trick for higher-order DEs.*\n\n*   **Hour 1-2.5: Bernoulli \u0026 Riccati DEs (Ch 2.4 \u0026 2.5)**\n    *   *Bernoulli Form:* $y\u0027 + f(x)y \u003d g(x)y^\\alpha$. *Recipe:* Divide by $y^\\alpha$ and substitute $z \u003d y^{1-\\alpha}$. It turns into a standard Linear DE!\n    *   *Riccati Form:* $y\u0027 \u003d a(x)y^2 + b(x)y + c(x)$. *Recipe:* If you are given *one* particular solution $y_1$, substitute $y \u003d y_1 + z$. It turns into a Bernoulli DE!\n*   **Hour 2.5-4: Clairaut \u0026 Lagrange DEs (Ch 2.6 \u0026 2.7)**\n    *   These are weird ones where you substitute $y\u0027 \u003d t$ and differentiate everything to get parametric solutions. Just memorize the steps.\n*   **Hour 4-7: Higher Order Linear DEs with Constant Coefficients (Ch 3.2) 🔥 *CRITICAL***\n    *   *Form:* $y\u0027\u0027 + ay\u0027 + by \u003d f(x)$\n    *   *Recipe:* Turn derivatives into powers of $\\lambda$ (e.g., $y\u0027\u0027 \\to \\lambda^2$). Solve the quadratic equation $\\lambda^2 + a\\lambda + b \u003d 0$. The roots tell you if the solution uses $e^{kx}$, $\\sin(kx)$, or $\\cos(kx)$.\n\n### **Day 3: Wrapping Up \u0026 Real-World Physics** *~6.5 Hours*\n*Goal: Finish the theory and spend a massive chunk of time just practicing recognizing the equations.*\n\n*   **Hour 1-2.5: Euler\u0027s DE (Eulerjeva DE - Ch 3.3)**\n    *   *Form:* $x^2y\u0027\u0027 + axy\u0027 + by \u003d f(x)$ (Notice the $x$ power matches the derivative order).\n    *   *Recipe:* Substitute $x \u003d e^t$. It miraculously transforms into the constant-coefficient DE you learned on Day 2!\n*   **Hour 2.5-4: Applications (Uporaba - Ch 4)**\n    *   Look at how they set up Free Fall with Air Resistance (Prosti pad), Chemical Mass Action (Zakon o delovanju mas), and Springs (Vzmeti). You already understand the physics, so just see how they translate to math.\n*   **Hour 4-6.5: \"Identify \u0026 Solve\" Practice (Naloge - Ch 5)**\n    *   This is the most important 2.5 hours. Look at random equations in Chapter 5. **Don\u0027t even solve them all entirely.** Just look at them and say: *\"Ah, that\u0027s a Bernoulli, I need to use $z\u003dy^{1-\\alpha}$\"* or *\"That\u0027s a Separable one.\"* If you can identify them, you will pass the exam.\n\n---\n\n### How to execute this:\n1.       "text": "\n\n\nTake a deep breath. You are absolutely **not** fucked. \n\nThe reason it feels unintuitive is because math textbooks are written backwards. They show you the polished, perfect, sterile final proof instead of showing you the messy, human \"hack\" that created it. \n\nSince it\u0027s a theory exam, the professor doesn\u0027t want you to just memorize the Greek letters. They want to know if you understand the *story* of what the math is doing. \n\nLet\u0027s translate those two pages of theory into plain logic. Here is the actual story of Chapter 3.1.\n\n---\n\n### Theory Concept 1: \"Linear Independence\" (Linearna neodvisnost)\n\n**The Textbook Definition:** \n$C_1 y_1 + C_2 y_2 + \\dots + C_n y_n \u003d 0 \\iff C_1 \u003d C_2 \u003d \\dots \u003d C_n \u003d 0$\n\n**The Intuitive Story:**\nImagine a 2nd-order differential equation. Because it\u0027s 2nd-order, the \"solution space\" is a 2D plane. To walk anywhere on a 2D plane, you need two directions: say, one step North ($y_1$) and one step East ($y_2$). \n\nWhat if the two solutions you found were $y_1 \u003d \\text{North}$ and $y_2 \u003d \\text{North}$? You only have one direction. You are stuck on a 1D line. You don\u0027t have the full solution. \n\nSo, how do we mathematically test if $y_1$ and $y_2$ are *actually* pointing in different directions? \nWe ask this question: **\"Can I mix $y_1$ and $y_2$ together to perfectly cancel each other out and get back to 0?\"**\n\n*   **Scenario A (Dependent/Bad):** Let\u0027s say $y_1 \u003d e^x$ and $y_2 \u003d 5e^x$. They are the same \"direction\". I can mix them to get 0! I just multiply the first by $5$ and the second by $-1$. \n    $$5(e^x) - 1(5e^x) \u003d 0$$\n    Here, $C_1 \u003d 5$ and $C_2 \u003d -1$. Because I found numbers *other than zero* that made them cancel out, they are mathematically identical. They are **Linearly Dependent (linearno odvisni)**. This means we failed to find a full solution.\n\n*   **Scenario B (Independent/Good):** Let\u0027s say $y_1 \u003d \\sin(x)$ and $y_2 \u003d \\cos(x)$. Try to find numbers to make $C_1\\sin(x) + C_2\\cos(x) \u003d 0$ for *every* $x$. \n    You literally can\u0027t do it. The ONLY way to make that equal 0 is if you set $C_1 \u003d 0$ and $C_2 \u003d 0$. \n    Because $0$ and $0$ are the *only* way to kill the equation, they are completely unique from each other. They are **Linearly Independent (linearno neodvisni)**. \n\n**How to answer this on the theory exam:** \n\"We need linear independence to ensure our fundamental solutions ($y_1, y_2...$) cover the entire dimension of the solution space. The equation $C_1 y_1 + ... \u003d 0$ is just the test to prove that none of our solutions are hidden copies of each other.\"\n\n---\n\n### Theory Concept 2: The \"Variation of Constants\" Derivation (Variacija konstant)\n\nThis is on pages 33-34. It looks like a giant wall of algebra. It\u0027s actually one of the most famous \"hacks\" in math history (invented by Lagrange).\n\n**The Setup:**\nWe want to solve a 2nd-order equation: $y\u0027\u0027 + a y\u0027 + b y \u003d f(x)$.\nWe guess the solution is: $y_P \u003d C_1(x)y_1 + C_2(x)y_2$. \n\nTo plug this into the equation, we need to take the derivative $y_P\u0027$. Let\u0027s use the product rule:\n$$y_P\u0027 \u003d [C_1\u0027(x)y_1 + C_2\u0027(x)y_2] +[C_1(x)y_1\u0027 + C_2(x)y_2\u0027]$$\n\n**The Problem:**\nIf we stop here and take the *second* derivative ($y_P\u0027\u0027$) to plug into our equation, we are going to have to take the derivative of $C_1\u0027(x)$. That will create **$C_1\u0027\u0027(x)$**. \nWe are trying to solve for $C_1(x)$. If we introduce $C_1\u0027\u0027(x)$, we just created a brand new, horrible 2nd-order differential equation! We are making things worse!\n\n**The Hack (The Genius Idea):**\nLagrange realized something. We have **two** unknown variables ($C_1(x)$ and $C_2(x)$), but we are only trying to satisfy **one** equation ($y\u0027\u0027 + a y\u0027 + b y \u003d f(x)$). \n\nIn math, if you have 2 variables but only 1 constraint, you have *infinitely many choices*. You have an extra degree of freedom. This means **we are allowed to invent a second constraint of our own choosing to make our lives easier.**\n\nWhat constraint should we invent? Well, we really hate that $[C_1\u0027 y_1 + C_2\u0027 y_2]$ bracket, because it causes second derivatives. \nSo Lagrange said: **\"Let\u0027s just force that bracket to equal 0.\"**\n\n**The Result:**\n1. We artificially enforce: **$C_1\u0027 y_1 + C_2\u0027 y_2 \u003d 0$**. (This becomes Equation 1 in our system!)\n2. Because that part is now 0, our first derivative shrinks to just: $y_P\u0027 \u003d C_1 y_1\u0027 + C_2 y_2\u0027$.\n3. Now, when we take the second derivative ($y_P\u0027\u0027$), we only get $C_1\u0027$ and $C_2\u0027$. No second derivatives!\n4.       }, {

      }, {
        "text": "actually* pointing in different directions? \nWe ask this question: **\"Can I mix $y_1$ and $y"

      }, {
